title: The Dreams of ‘Star Trek’ Aren’t Dead
gist: Una McCormack contrasts NASA's April 2026 Artemis II mission — which broke Apollo 13's 1970 distance record at over 406,000 km from Earth — with billionaire spaceflight spectacle from Blue Origin and SpaceX, arguing space utopianism is contested ideological terrain rather than a settled commercial project. She reads Paramount's Star Trek franchise, particularly the cancelled Starfleet Academy, as a battleground over competing visions of the American future, and invokes David Graeber's poetic-versus-bureaucratic technology distinction to frame who gets to decide what the future is built for.

themes.theme: Artemis II versus billionaire spaceflight spectacle

insights.claim: NASA's four-person Artemis II crew traveled more than 406,000 kilometers from Earth in April 2026, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: State-run deep-space capability just set a 56-year record — a concrete counterpoint to the narrative that public space programs have been eclipsed by private launch.
insights.quote: The four-person crew of NASA’s Artemis II mission broke the record set by Apollo 13, back in 1970, traveling more than 406,000 kilometers from Earth.

insights.claim: Billionaire-funded space missions have delivered celebrity suborbital passengers via Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin and a launched flying car via Elon Musk's SpaceX, while NASA offered a sober vision built on an earnest representative crew and the promise of future lunar surface missions.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: The legitimacy contest between public and private space programs is being fought on symbolism, which shapes political support and therefore NASA budget allocation.

insights.claim: The current crop of moonshots has revealed a deep ideological divide over who should undertake space exploration and what should be done once out there, making space utopianism a contested rather than consensual project.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Space policy is now a values fight, not just a procurement fight — the risk to commercial space is political legitimacy, not engineering.

themes.theme: Star Trek as contested American IP

insights.claim: Star Trek has functioned as a battlefield for warring visions of the American dream, with battles for intellectual control over its cultural legacy becoming increasingly pointed sixty years after its first transmission.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Legacy IP is now politically polarized terrain, which raises reputational and audience-fragmentation risk for the studios that own it.

insights.claim: Star Trek: Discovery, which premiered in 2017, drew accusations of wokeness from the moment it opened by foregrounding two women of color, and the latest franchise entry Starfleet Academy has been subject to vituperative review-bombing.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Coordinated review-bombing is a measurable demand-side risk to franchise extensions — audience scores can now be manufactured against a title before it finds viewers.

insights.claim: Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir publicly dismissed almost the entirety of the Star Trek franchise's recent offerings as worthless, stating a preference for watching Romulans and the Federation shoot at each other.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Even genre insiders now demand conflict-driven rather than utopian science fiction — a signal about what commissioning committees will greenlight next.

insights.claim: Recent iterations of Paramount's most enduring and successful IP have tended toward nostalgia, with Discovery establishing lead Michael Burnham as Spock's adopted sister and that move leading directly to the commissioning of Strange New Worlds set aboard the Enterprise under Christopher Pike.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Franchise economics reward retroactive continuity over new invention — the value is being harvested from the back catalogue rather than created.

themes.theme: Roddenberry's progressive legacy and its real-world effects

insights.claim: Nichelle Nichols's presence as Uhura on the Star Trek bridge inspired a young Mae Jemison to become an astronaut, and Nichols was dissuaded from quitting the show by Martin Luther King Jr.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Documented case of screen representation converting into actual STEM career pipeline — the mechanism behind arguments for casting decisions as policy.

insights.claim: The 1968 Star Trek episode 'Plato's Stepchildren' contained one of the first interracial kisses on U.S. television, only a year after Loving v. Virginia struck down laws banning interracial marriage.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Popular entertainment ran roughly one year behind the legal frontier on race — a benchmark for how fast mass media follows institutional change.

insights.claim: The moneyless and post-scarcity aspects of the Federation were foregrounded in The Next Generation in the late 1980s, establishing considered utopianism as an explicit part of the franchise's economics.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: The most successful mainstream depiction of a post-scarcity economy came from the late Cold War era — worth revisiting as AI-abundance narratives look for cultural precedent.

themes.theme: Patrilineality, the Borg, and reactionary drift

insights.claim: Picard's third season concluded with the unintentionally reactionary revelation that a younger generation of Starfleet cadets had been affected by the individuality-stripping Borg and could only be freed by the wisdom of their elders, a plot strangely evocative of far-right paranoia about the 'woke mind virus'.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Nostalgia-driven storytelling can smuggle in the politics it means to oppose — a reputational hazard for legacy IP revivals.

insights.claim: Star Trek repeatedly reaffirms patrilineality as its central dynamic of interest, from Spock and Sarek to Picard and Maurice to the Wrath of Khan revelation of Kirk's son David Marcus, mirroring a father-son focus so pervasive across U.S. film and television as to constitute a cliché.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: A structural template that governs what stories mainstream American media will fund, and therefore what it structurally cannot say.

insights.claim: The tender relationship between Benjamin Sisko and his son Jake in Deep Space Nine is a rare exception to Trek's difficult-father pattern, and is partly attributable to actor Avery Brooks's insistence on representing a positive and loving relationship between a Black man and his son.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Individual creative insistence, not institutional policy, produced the franchise's most notable counter-example — representation depends on people with leverage using it.

themes.theme: Starfleet Academy as post-collapse reconstruction parable

insights.claim: Starfleet Academy is set in the 32nd century after a cataclysmic event called 'the Burn' caused the near-collapse of the United Federation of Planets, following the first cohort of cadets admitted since that collapse.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Mainstream science fiction has shifted its premise from expansion to reconstruction after institutional collapse — a tell about the cultural mood.
insights.locator: The series is set in the far future

insights.claim: The casting of former Georgia gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams as the president of United Earth in Discovery's final season signals that the Federation's attempted reconstitution is meant to be read as the United States approaching its 250th anniversary.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: The franchise is explicitly allegorizing American institutional decline and renewal at the semiquincentennial — a read on elite cultural anxiety heading into 2026.

insights.claim: Starfleet Academy refocuses the franchise's central dynamic from father-son conflict onto matrilineality and mothering as significant work, through the relationship between chancellor Nahla Ake and Caleb Mir, a young delinquent whom a Federation court separated from his mother at an early age.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: A deliberate structural break from the American media template — and it was the show that got cancelled.

insights.claim: Starfleet Academy has been cancelled despite using Trek's heritage to tell stories about reconstructing a collapsed polity on values of mutuality and care.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Studios are retiring the utopian-reconstruction format even inside a franchise built on it — the commissioning environment favors conflict.
insights.quote: It is a shame—with the show’s perhaps inevitable cancellation—that we will not get to see more of how this might have played out.

insights.claim: David Graeber's 2015 book The Utopia of Rules distinguishes poetic technologies — the use of rational technical means to bring wild impossible fantasies to life, such as moonshots, vaccinations and terraforming — from bureaucratic technologies that produce ever-increasing means of administrating ourselves.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: A usable classifier for any technology investment: does it enlarge the possible, or only extend administration and control?
insights.quote: the use of rational, technical … means to bring wild, impossible fantasies to life
insights.locator: In a 2015 book, The Utopia of Rules

insights.claim: Graeber argues the purpose of bureaucratic technologies is greater labor discipline, increased surveillance and the furtherance of governability or social control, determining who gets to inhabit the future and who gets to go to the moon.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Frames the surveillance and workforce-management technology stack as a distinct category with its own political economy, separate from frontier tech.
insights.locator: Against these, he contrasts bureaucratic technologies

insights.claim: The same poetic-technology capability that can deliver moonshots, vaccination and peace can equally deliver a gilded luxury resort on the dark side of the moon and longevity for a chosen few — the outcome is a choice rather than a property of the technology.
insights.speaker: Una McCormack
insights.so_what: Capability is neutral; distribution is political — the core argument that will shape regulation of space, longevity and AI.
